title: Assessment of prenatal exposure to arsenic in Tenerife Island.
ehr_evidence: Neonatal meconium was collected from the infant's diaper and total arsenic was quantified by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES); a structured questionnaire on sociodemographic, lifestyle and dietary habits during pregnancy was administered the day after delivery.
summary: A cross-sectional descriptive pilot study of 96 mother-child pairs in Tenerife, Spain, assessing prenatal arsenic exposure via meconium analysis and examining associations with maternal diet/lifestyle and neonatal outcomes.
key_findings: Total arsenic was detected in 37 (38.5%) of 96 meconium samples, with a range of 0.10 to 31.40 ng/g.

Frequent intake of vegetables was associated with prenatal arsenic exposure (OR 1.19; 95% CI 1.01-1.41) and remained the only factor significantly and independently associated in the adjusted multivariate model (OR 1.31; 95% CI 1.02-1.68).
Low weekly intake of eggs was associated with prenatal arsenic exposure (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.34-0.94).
Frequent intake of processed meat showed a non-significant trend toward arsenic exposure (OR 8.54; 95% CI 0.80-90.89).

No significant association was found between meconium arsenic and obstetric or neonatal outcomes, with the exception of a significantly higher birth weight in exposed newborns (OR 1.00; 95% CI 1.00-1.02).
Arsenic concentration was significantly correlated only with average consumption of white meat (Spearman's rho -0.45; p = 0.02).
captured_features: Total arsenic concentration in meconium (ng/g, ppb)
Maternal dietary habits via 16-item food frequency questionnaire
Maternal lifestyle factors (tobacco smoke, alcohol, medicine use, chemical exposure)
Sociodemographic variables (maternal/father education, social class, age, country of origin, area of residence)
Neonatal outcomes (birth weight, gestational age, length, cranial perimeter, prematurity, clinical diagnosis)
pathologies_diseases: No significant neonatal pathologies; only birth weight was significantly associated with arsenic exposure
population: 96 pregnant women and their newborns in Tenerife, Spain; enrolled August 2006 to June 2007
limitations: No data on arsenic speciation, so inorganic versus organic arsenic exposure could not be differentiated, risking overestimation of health risk.
Small sample size and single-island setting make results difficult to generalize.
Poor correlation between detected arsenic and food consumption, likely because intake was expressed as frequency per week rather than mg/day/person.
ICP-OES used rather than atomic absorption spectrometry, and the small meconium amount precluded arsenic speciation.
